extracted.intended_audience: novelists, serious fiction writers, and critics studying fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling point of view and the modes of treatment (dramatic scene vs pictorial/narrative) in a novel, including how and when to use first/third person, oblique narration, scenes, and panoramic picture. Useful for planning a book's development and handling key turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic method / picture-making
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of picture-making when it uses the dramatic method: letting events and actions 'tell their own story' rather than being told by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatization (showing) where possible: let scenes, dialogue, and conduct constitute the occasion. Avoid narrating what can be acted out, because dramatic presentation gives the sharpest, most vivid effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration necessary for summary or long spans
rubrics_metrics.description: There are occasions when the general effect of a long period (e.g. a year in a man's life) cannot be wholly acted and must be given as somebody's narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summary/oblique narration to render broad sweeps of time or accumulated impressions economically; do not attempt to dramatize everything at full length.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person POV: fixed spatial/temporal limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story is told in the first person 'there can, of course, be no uncertainty in the point of view; he has his fixed position, he cannot leave it.' The field of vision is defined with distinctness and the story cannot stray outside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that first-person narration fixes you in one consciousness and perspective; it prevents the narrator from describing events outside his experience and can limit dramatic scope and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person POV: spatially fixed but temporally free
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing to the third person retains a fixed seeing-eye in space but frees the narration in time: 'All the variety obtainable by a shifting relation to the story in time is thus in the author's hand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use third-person (even when tied to a character's vision) to manipulate temporal distance — far retrospect, present urgency, or gradations between — without changing the seeing-eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique narration / authorial reinforcement of character vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The author may adopt a character's field of vision while supplementing it: 'there are now two brains behind that eye' — the character's and the author's — so the picture becomes richer without a double point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ oblique narration to keep apparent fidelity to a character's perspective while unobtrusively adding authorial detail, deepening impressions without breaking the established POV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edging away from the seer: closing a character's consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The author can 'imperceptibly edge away from the seer' and 'allow his hero’s act of vision to lapse' so that the character becomes impenetrable and stands among others as an objective presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intermittent closure of the narrator's consciousness to let the protagonist participate in scenes as an actor among equals (dialogue, action) and to avoid the protagonist dissolving into an over-subjective blur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant-reporting weakens true drama
rubrics_metrics.description: When a participant in an event reports it, 'a scene of true drama is impossible' because the reporter's contribution has a different quality and lacks the crispness of direct drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on strict first-person participant reports for moments intended to function as true dramatic scenes; if drama is desired, present the scene rather than have it reported by an actor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minstrel's licence (authorial narrator) is often the easy way
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an 'immemorial' way where the author speaks directly to the reader and imposes no limitation on freedom; while sometimes effective, this is often the easiest and narrowest method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of choosing omniscient-authorial voice merely because it is easy; a disciplined method tailored to the story usually yields better results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view choice must be disciplined and serve the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The only worthwhile approach is 'the way by which the most is made of the story to be told' — a choice and disciplined method rather than the easy way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide POV with purpose: the selection should maximize what can be achieved with the subject, enabling the most effective use of dramatic and pictorial instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene (dramatic incident) is primary in importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incident, the scene 'comes first in importance, beyond doubt' — novelists instinctively see chief turns as acted scenes because they are the sharpest effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and place scenes strategically; they deliver the clearest, most forceful effects in a novel and should be prioritized when emphasis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene limitations: time/space cannot be foreshortened; scenes are expensive
rubrics_metrics.description: In a scene 'there can be no foreshortening of time or space' — a scene displays the whole time and space it occupies and is therefore expensive in length and slow relative to its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that scenes take up narrative time; prepare scenes in advance with prior narration or picture so they are not taxed with work they cannot do; avoid gratuitous or wasteful dramatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scenes to clinch, demonstrate, and crown effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene should be used 'to clinch a matter already pending, to demonstrate a result, to crown an effect half-made by other means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve full dramatic scenes for moments that require their unique force — climaxes, revelations, confirmations — rather than using scenes for mundane exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture / panoramic method as complementary to drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture (the general survey) 'finds its opportunity where a long reach is more needed than sharp visibility' and 'travels over periods and expanses' to accumulate impressions for drama to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use panoramic/narrative picture to cover wide scope, accumulate impression, and economize time; let picture prepare or supplement scenes rather than substitute for drama in climactic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert pictorial weakness into strength by dramatizing the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The inherent thinness of pictorial report should be admitted and then 'asserted and emphasized' — dramatize the mirror (the narrator's mind) so the report becomes a distinct object of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using reports or interior presentation, make the narrator's consciousness itself vivid and dramatized so that the reflection (the mind) is a defined, powerful object rather than a thin copy of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical method: study the technical making of books
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should fasten upon the question of a novel's making: 'the critic must overtake him at his work and see how the book was made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For readers and critics: analyze the craft and technical devices (POV, scene placement, picture vs drama) in order to recreate and understand novels; surface praise of talent is insufficient.
